segments.translit: tam evārtha[ṃ] paramārthāya saṃvṛtisatyārthāvagame kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ ḍombīsandhyayā pratipādayanti(ti)—
segments.translation: [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} sets out this same meaning in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of [Ḍombī]{dombi}, for the sake of the [ultimate]{paramartha}, in understanding the meaning of [conventional]{samvrti} truth:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} (Kāṇha) sets out the same meaning in the [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} of [Ḍombī]{dombi}, for the sake of the [ultimate]{paramartha}, in understanding [conventional]{samvrti} truth. The Tibetan instead has him speak having understood both truths, ultimate and conventional (cp.18.m1).

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads don dam pa dang kun rdzob kyi bden pa'i don khong du chud pas, 'having understood the meaning of the ultimate and the conventional truths': it coordinates the two truths and makes the understanding the poet's own, where the Sanskrit has paramārthāya, 'for the sake of the ultimate', beside a locative, saṃvṛtisatyārthāvagame, 'in understanding the meaning of conventional truth'. I follow the Sanskrit. The Tibetan dgongs pa'i skad, 'intentional language', confirms that sandhyayā here means the twilight language.
pratipādayanti(ti): Shastri's parenthesis marks a doubtful syllable; the sense, 'sets out', is not affected. The honorific plural kṛṣṇācāryyapādāḥ is rendered as a singular.
tam evārthaṃ, 'this same meaning', points back to what earlier songs taught; which song or teaching is not said.

segments.translit: tiṇītyādi| mayā kṛṣṇācāryyeṇa vajravanitābhiṣva(sa)ṅgāt tribhuvanaṃ kāyavākcittaṃ| tasya ṣaṣṭyuttaraśataprakṛtidoṣo 'vahelayā bādhitaḥ| ata evāhaṃ suptaḥ| līlem iti krīḍayā yoganidrāṃ gataḥ| nairātmadharmmāvagamāt|
segments.translation: “Three…” and so on. By me, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, through attachment to the [vajra woman]{vajravanita}: the [three worlds]{trailokya} are [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}, and their fault of the hundred and sixty [natures]{prakrti} was overcome with ease. That is why I am asleep. “In the play” means in play: I went into [yogic sleep]{yoganidra} through understanding the nature of [selflessness]{nairatmya}.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the [three worlds]{trailokya} as [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}. Through attachment to the [vajra woman]{vajravanita}, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} says, he overcame the fault of the hundred and sixty [natures]{prakrti} with ease: bādhita, 'overcome', stands where the song has 'rowed'. So he sleeps: in [play]{lila} he entered [yogic sleep]{yoganidra}, understanding the nature of [selflessness]{nairatmya} (cp.18.m2).

flags.note: bādhitaḥ, 'overcome, checked', and avahelayā, 'with ease', stand where the song has bāhia helem̐ (draft: 'rowed … with ease'): the gloss seems to hear bāhia as bādhita. The Tibetan comment agrees ('bad pa med pas 'gog pa, 'stopped without effort'), and its line has 'bad med 'jug, 'enter without effort'. There is no explicit iti-gloss, and the draft line is left as it is.
abhiṣva(sa)ṅgāt: Shastri offers abhisaṅga beside the printed abhiṣvaṅga; both mean attachment or close union. The Tibetan mngon par chags pa, 'attachment', fits either.

The Tibetan has sa gsum gyi lus dang ngag dang yid, 'the body, speech and mind of the three worlds', a genitive where the Sanskrit sets the three worlds and body, speech and mind in apposition; and nyal nas 'jug pa, 'having lain down, enters', for suptaḥ, 'asleep'.

For nairātmadharmāvagamāt, 'through understanding the nature of selflessness', the Tibetan has bdag med ma'i chos khong du chud pa, 'understood the dharma of Nairātmā' (the goddess), joined by 'and' rather than given as the cause; for yoganidrā it has rnal 'byor pa gnyid, 'the yogi's sleep'.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadenāpariśuddhāvadhūtikām upagamayati—
kaisaṇītyādi| bharbhariālikā asadāropeṇa bho ḍombini pariśu[28ka]ddhāvadhūtikā kiṃ kṛtaṃ tvayā| kau śarīre līnaṃ yat prabhāsvaraṃ yad ajñānarasenānte bāhye kṛtaṃ| kaṃ saṃvṛttibo[dhi]cittaṃ pālayatīti kṛtvā kāpālikaś cittavajra-ādhānaṃ kṛtam iti|
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he presents the impure [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}:
“What kind…” and so on. [Bharbhariālikā]{bhabhariali}: by false [imputation]{aropa}. “O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, pure [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, what have you done?” The [clear light]{prabhasvara} that is dissolved in ku, in the [body]{body}, is the one that the juice of ignorance has put “at the edge”, outside. On the ground that he protects ka, [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, he is the [kāpālika]{kapalika}: he has set in place the [vajra of mind]{trivajra}.
segments.note: Munidatta hears the [refrain]{dhruvapada} as addressed to [Ḍombī]{dombi} as the impure [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} (the central channel); her [bhābhariālī]{bhabhariali} (sense uncertain) goes with false [imputation]{aropa}. He seems to split kuliṇa as ku-līna: [clear light]{prabhasvara} dissolved in the body, put outside by ignorance. The [kāpālika]{kapalika} is one who protects ka, [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} ('mind of awakening'), setting the [vajra of mind]{trivajra} in place (cp.18.m3).

equations.en: one who protects (pālayati) ka, conventional bodhicitta

flags.note: Shastri prints pariśu[28ka]ddhāvadhūtikā, 'pure avadhūtī', in the vocative. The segment's own introduction has apariśuddhāvadhūtikām, 'the impure avadhūtī', cp.18.m4 has ḍombinyā 'pariśuddhāvadhūtikayā, and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has yongs su ma dag pa'i a wa d+hU tI pa, 'impure', in both places. An initial a- has probably been lost (apariśuddhā-, perhaps swallowed in sandhi after ḍombini). Translated as printed; see questions.

upagamayati, literally 'causes to approach': 'presents', 'addresses' or 'makes known'. The Tibetan has khro bar byed pa, 'rebukes, angers', which suits the uparāgayati of cp.18.m4 better and may reflect a different verb.

bharbhariālikā (the song's bhābhariālī) stands beside asadāropeṇa, 'by false imputation', with no verb and no iti, so there is no explicit equation; the words may paraphrase the refrain's question ('what bharbhariālikā have you made by false imputation?'). The Tibetan has skra yags ('fine hair') … mi rtag par sgro 'dogs pas, 'by imputing impermanence'.

kau śarīre līnaṃ, 'dissolved in ku (earth), in the body', seems to split the refrain's kuliṇa(jaṇa) as ku + līna, and bāhye, 'outside', glosses the song's ante, 'at the edge'. Neither is stated as a gloss. kau is taken as the locative of ku, 'earth', in apposition to śarīre. The Tibetan (gang zhig lus la thim na) has only 'in the body'.

For ajñānarasena, 'by the juice of ignorance', the Tibetan has 'od gsal mi shes pa'i dbang gis, 'through not knowing clear light', with no 'juice' and with clear light as what is not known; it also makes what is put outside plural (de rnams).
The Tibetan breaks off mid-sentence (… skyong bar byed pa'i phyir ka pA la ni) before cittavajra-ādhānaṃ kṛtam, and does not show the syllable ka on which the kāpālika etymology turns.

segments.translit:
viśiṣya padāntareṇa tām evoparāgayati—
tam̐i lo ityādi| tayā ḍombinyā 'pariśuddhāvadhūtikayā devāsuramanuṣyāditraidhātukaṃ sakalaṃ mithyājñānena ṭālitam iti nāśitam| yata eva śaśaharaṃ saṃvṛttibodhicittaṃ prabhāsvarahetubhūtaṃ| asampradāyayoginyā ṭālitam iti vinaṣṭīkṛtaṃ|
tathā ca caryyāpādāḥ—
khālata paṛilem̐ kāpura nāśaye ityādi|
segments.translation:
With the next [verse]{pada} he censures that same woman in particular:
“You…” and so on. By that [Ḍombī]{dombi}, the impure [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, the whole of the [three worlds]{trailokya}, of gods, asuras, humans and the rest, has been ṭālita, that is, destroyed, through [false knowledge]{mithyajnana}, precisely because the [moon]{moon}, [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, which is the cause of [clear light]{prabhasvara}, has been ṭālita, that is, ruined, by the [yoginī]{yogini} without the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}.
And so the Caryā masters: “Fallen into a ditch, [camphor]{camphor} perishes,” and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta takes 'everything' as the threefold world of gods, asuras and humans, which [Ḍombī]{dombi}, the impure [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, has destroyed through [false knowledge]{mithyajnana}. The [moon]{moon} is [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}; the song's 'cause of deeds' becomes 'cause of [clear light]{prabhasvara}', ruined by the [yoginī]{yogini} without the [guru's lineage]{guru-sampradaya}. He quotes a Caryā line: [camphor]{camphor} fallen into a ditch perishes (cp.18.m4).

equations.en: conventional bodhicitta, the cause of clear light

citations.work: Unidentified Old Bengali caryā line, cited from 'the Caryā masters' (caryāpādāḥ); the Tibetan attributes it to glu dbyangs zhabs, 'the Song master'

flags.note: uparāgayati: 'colours, affects', or 'reviles, censures' (uparāga also means an eclipse, apt beside the toppled moon). I render 'censures'. The Tibetan parallel has neither this introductory sentence nor the lemma tam̐i lo.

yata eva … ṭālitam is a 'because' clause with no main clause of its own; I read it as giving the reason the three worlds are destroyed. It could also be taken as 'for which very reason'. The Tibetan has gang de nyid 'joms pa ni, 'as for what destroys that very thing'.

For asampradāyayoginyā, 'by the yoginī without the guru's lineage', the Tibetan has man ngag dang bral ba'i rnal 'byor pas, 'by the yogin lacking the instruction': masculine, and 'instruction' for 'lineage'. The compound itself may mean a yoginī who lacks the lineage or the yoginī of those who lack it.
prabhāsvarahetubhūtaṃ, 'which is the cause of clear light', stands where the song has kājaṇa kāraṇa, 'the cause of deeds': a paraphrase, not an explicit gloss.

The quoted line khālata paṛilem̐ kāpura nāśaye is Old Bengali and is not part of this song; its source is not identified. caryāpādāḥ may be an honorific for one author or mean 'the Caryā masters'; the Tibetan glu dbyangs zhabs, 'the Song master', is close to nag po glu dbyangs zhabs, which the glossary records as a Tibetan name for Kāṇha. nāśaye is taken as 'perishes'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena ḍombī[mbi]svarūpam āha—
keho ityādi| ye 'pi svarūpānabhijñā[ḥ] sahajānandapariśuddhitayā tvāṃ ḍombī[ṃ] na jānanti| te 'pi karmmavasitāṃ prāpya saṃsāraduḥkhānubhavāt tava viruddhaṃ vadanti| ye te prādeśikā yogīndrāḥ samyakvajrājasaṃyoga[ā]kṣarasukhatayā tvāṃ prajānanti| te 'pi kaṇṭhe sambhogacakre aharniśan na parityajantī[ti] [29]|
tathā cāgamaḥ—
kakkolapriyabolamelakatayā 'nandasphuratkundarāḥ
sadyaḥ śodhitaśālilālitakarā[ḥ] kāliñjarāś cakriṇaḥ||
bhraśyaddivyasarojapātramadanavyāluptadantacchadāḥ
pretāvāsanivāsanityarasikāḥ kecit kvacit yoginaḥ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of [Ḍombī]{dombi}:
“Some…” and so on. Those who, not knowing the true nature, do not know you, Ḍombī, as the purity of [innate joy]{sahajananda}: they too, having come under the sway of karma, speak against you because they experience the suffering of [saṃsāra]{samsara}. Those [lords of yogis]{yogindra}, found here and there, who know you fully as the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of the perfect union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}: they do not let go of you at the [neck]{kantha}, the [wheel of enjoyment]{sambhoga-cakra}, by day or by night.
And so the [scripture]{agama}:
“Their [kundura]{kundura} throbbing with [joy]{ananda} as [kakkola]{kakkola} meets dear [bola]{bola},
their hands at once playing in cleansed rice, [kāliñjaras]{kalinjara}, members of the circle,
their lips rubbed bare by the intoxicant of the divine lotus-cup as it tips,
ever delighting in a [dwelling]{nivasa} in the abode of the dead: such, here and there, are some [yogis]{yogi}.”
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse gives [Ḍombī]{dombi}'s [true nature]{svarupa}. Those who do not know her as the purity of [innate joy]{sahajananda} speak against her; the few [lords of yogis]{yogindra} who know her through the [imperishable bliss]{aksara-sukha} of vajra and lotus united never let go of her [neck]{kantha}, the [wheel of enjoyment]{sambhoga-cakra}. He quotes a verse on rare cremation-ground yogis (cp.18.m5).

citations.quoted: kakkolapriyabolamelakatayā 'nandasphuratkundarāḥ / sadyaḥ śodhitaśālilālitakarāḥ kāliñjarāś cakriṇaḥ / bhraśyaddivyasarojapātramadanavyāluptadantacchadāḥ / pretāvāsanivāsanityarasikāḥ kecit kvacit yoginaḥ

flags.note: karmmavasitāṃ is printed; read karmavaśitāṃ, 'subjection to karma' (Bengali s for ś), as the Tibetan las kyi dbang gis, 'by the power of karma', supports.
vajrāja is printed, taken as vajrābja, 'vajra and lotus', as with kuliśāja elsewhere in the commentary; the Tibetan has rdo rje dang pad+ma.

For svarūpānabhijñāḥ, 'not knowing the true nature', the Tibetan has rang bzhin gyis mngon par shes pa, 'knowing directly by nature', without the negative, and it attaches the purity of innate joy to Ḍombī herself (lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba yongs su dag pa'i Dom+bi ni).

The Tibetan has 'gul ba ('movement') for kaṇṭhe, apparently for mgul ba, 'neck'; rig par bya'o, 'are to be known', for prajānanti, 'know'; and phyogs gcig tu for prādeśika, which I render 'found here and there' (literally 'local, partial').

The quoted verse (śārdūlavikrīḍita) is obscure. kakkola, bola, kundura and kāliñjara are kept in source form; melaka ('meeting', possibly a tantric gathering), madana ('intoxicant') and pretāvāsa ('abode of the dead') are rendered literally. cakriṇaḥ may be 'members of the circle' or 'wheel-bearers' (Tibetan 'khor lo can). śodhitaśālilālitakarāḥ is uncertain, here 'hands playing in cleansed rice'; the Tibetan has chu yis sbyor zhing lag pa 'khrid pa, 'joined with water and leading by the hand', as if reading salila, 'water'.

vyālupta, 'rubbed away, effaced', of the lips; the Tibetan rnam pa kun du chags, 'clinging all over', may reflect vyālipta, 'smeared'. The Tibetan also has mtsho skyes 'dab ma'i btung ba, 'the drink of the lotus petals', for sarojapātra, 'lotus-cup'.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena yoginyānuśaṃsām āha—kāhne gāi ityādi| īdṛśī karmmasthasādhanopāyacaṇḍālī kṛṣṇācāryyaiḥ paraṃ gīyate nānyaiḥ| ḍombīvyatirekāt nānyā cchinnanāsikā nāgarikā vā vidyate| yasmāt sattvabhedaṃ prāpya bhedādhiṣṭhānaṃ vidhatte|
tathā ca jñānasaṃbodhau—
cittam eva mahābījaṃ bhavanirvvāṇayor api|
saṃvṛtau saṃvṛtiṃ yāti nirvvāṇe niḥsvabhāvatām|| 18||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the [praise]{anusamsa} of the [yoginī]{yogini}: “[Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has sung…” and so on. Such a [Caṇḍālī]{candali}, the means of practice for one who abides in action, is sung by [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} alone, and by no one else. Apart from [Ḍombī]{dombi} there is no other woman whose nose has been cut off, or woman of the town, for, taking on the differences among beings, she creates a basis for difference.
And so in the [Jñānasaṃbodhi]{tx-jnanasambodhi}:
“The [mind]{citta} alone is the great seed of both [existence]{bhava} and [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}.
In the [conventional]{samvrti} it becomes the conventional; in nirvāṇa it becomes [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}.”
segments.note: Munidatta says [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} alone sings such a [Caṇḍālī]{candali}, 'the means of practice for one who abides in action' (an obscure phrase). Apart from [Ḍombī]{dombi} there is no other woman with her nose cut off, or woman of the town, since she takes on beings' differences. He quotes the [Jñānasaṃbodhi]{tx-jnanasambodhi}: [mind]{citta} alone is the seed of [existence]{bhava} and [nirvāṇa]{nirvana} (cp.18.m6).

equations.en: a woman whose nose has been cut off, or a woman of the town

citations.quoted: cittam eva mahābījaṃ bhavanirvāṇayor api | saṃvṛtau saṃvṛtiṃ yāti nirvāṇe niḥsvabhāvatām
citations.work: Jñānasaṃbodhi (named by Munidatta, cp.18.m6; not otherwise identified)

flags.note: karmasthasādhanopāya is obscure: 'the means of practice for one who abides in action' follows the glossary; 'the means of accomplishing what rests on action' is also possible. It stands where the song has kāma, 'desire', perhaps read as karma. The Tibetan has las kyi gnas sgrub pa'i thabs, 'the means of accomplishing the place of action', and gzhan du blangs, 'sung elsewhere', for paraṃ gīyate, 'is sung only'.

The Tibetan has 'apart from Ḍombī there is no other low-caste woman (dmangs rigs), yet there is the town woman herself (grong khyer ma nyid yod pa'o)': it renders cchinnanāsikā with its word for the song's chiṇālī, not 'nose cut off', and turns nāgarikā into a positive statement instead of a second alternative.

yasmāt sattvabhedaṃ prāpya bhedādhiṣṭhānaṃ vidhatte is obscure and its subject unexpressed (Ḍombī, or the mind of the verse that follows): 'taking on the differences among beings, she creates a basis for difference'; adhiṣṭhāna may also mean 'blessing'. The Tibetan has sems can gyi dbye bas thob par bya ba'i gnas yod pa'o, 'there is a place to be attained through the divisions of beings'.
The Tibetan renders the Jñānasaṃbodhi verse loosely, as prose (kun rdzob la kun rdzob kyi phyir …; mya ngan las 'das pa'i ngo bo nyid mi gnas pa'o, 'the nature of nirvāṇa does not abide').

questions: cp.18.m3: Shastri prints pariśu[28ka]ddhāvadhūtikā, 'pure avadhūtī', in the vocative, but the segment's own introduction (apariśuddhāvadhūtikām), cp.18.m4 (ḍombinyā 'pariśuddhāvadhūtikayā) and the Tibetan (yongs su ma dag pa'i, twice) all have 'impure'. I translated what is printed and flagged a probable lost a-. Should the translation be emended to 'impure', or keep the printed 'pure' with the flag?

cp.18.m3: kau śarīre līnaṃ ('dissolved in ku, in the body') looks like a split of the refrain's kuliṇa as ku + līna, with the song's ante glossed as bāhye, 'outside'. The kulina glossary entry says Munidatta does not comment on the word. Should that entry record this implied reading, marked as a paraphrase rather than an explicit gloss (cp.18.m3)?

cp.18.m2: Munidatta's bādhitaḥ, 'overcome', stands where the song has bāhia, and the Tibetan comment agrees ('bad pa med pas 'gog pa). The draft keeps 'rowed' in 1a; do you want a note on the line (cp.18.m2)?

Person markup: I rendered Munidatta's own form Kṛṣṇācārya as [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} (cp.18.m1, cp.18.m2, cp.18.m6) and the song's Kāṇha as [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, although the entry's English is 'Kāṇha'. Is that the convention you want?

Approved renderings that do not fit Munidatta's words: chinali ('loose woman') cannot carry his cchinnanāsikā, 'woman whose nose has been cut off' (cp.18.m6), so I left it unmarked and recorded the gloss under equations; carya ('conduct') does not fit caryāpādāḥ, left unmarked as 'the Caryā masters' (cp.18.m4); for kantha I kept 'neck' for kaṇṭhe, though he means the wheel at the throat (cp.18.m5). Acceptable?

cp.18.m5: in the scriptural verse I kept kakkola, bola, kundura and kāliñjara in source form, as the glossary directs, and rendered the obscure second line (śodhitaśālilālitakarāḥ) literally, as 'hands playing in cleansed rice'; the Tibetan reads it quite differently (water, leading by the hand). Would you rather have a literal rendering with the flag, as now, or the line marked as untranslatable (cp.18.m5)?

cp.18.m4: I rendered uparāgayati 'censures' (other senses: 'colours, affects'; uparāga is also 'eclipse'). Is the quoted camphor line (khālata paṛilem̐ kāpura nāśaye) known to you from another song or dohā? The Tibetan ascribes it to glu dbyangs zhabs, which may mean Kāṇha (cp.18.m4).
